what: Two wheel motors move the chassis; a third tilts its distance-sensor head. Gravity back-drives the sensor head unless the motor actively holds its position.
try: Reset and run the short out-and-back survey.
Watch the sensor head when the motor changes between motion and holding.
Stop the program, change its head angle gently and compare the sensing direction.
why: Gravity exerts a torque on the offset head. An active position hold can oppose it; merely braking a motor does not guarantee a fixed angle. Sensor direction changes with the head pose.
matters: Robot sensors need stable mounting and a known viewing direction.
question: Is a zero speed command always the same as holding a position?
answer: No. Holding uses position feedback to provide a balancing torque. Passive braking can allow gravity-driven drift.
further: Compare the head while driving and while stationary.
Relate the distance reading to the ray direction, not just the chassis heading.
formula: gravity torque = mass × gravity × perpendicular lever arm
